questions.title: What standard does the Federal Circuit apply when reviewing a district court’s denial of a JMOL of noninfringement?
questions.question_body: In the opinion, the court says it reviews denials of JMOL de novo under Fifth Circuit law, citing Wi‑LAN and Apple cases. I’m confused about how the de novo standard works in practice: does the appellate court look at the evidence itself, or only at whether the district court made a legal error? How does the “substantial evidence” test interact with the de novo review?

questions.title: How should the claim term “signals of interest” be construed under the ’134 patent, and why was the expert’s testimony considered insufficient?
questions.question_body: The court discusses the expert mapping the downlink TX reference to “signals of interest” and the modeled PIM path to “interference generating signals.” It then says the expert never actually linked x1/x2 to those claim terms. What is the proper construction of “signals of interest” under the patent, and why does the lack of a direct link cause the jury’s finding to lack substantial evidence?

questions.title: Why does the Federal Circuit consider the amendment to “three signals S1, S2, S3” in the ’775 patent not a clear disavowal of two‑signal embodiments?
questions.question_body: Finesse amended the claims during prosecution to recite three signals instead of “two or three signals.” The court says this is not a clear and unambiguous disavowal. What legal standard governs whether a claim amendment disavows prior claim scope, and how did the court apply it here?

questions.title: What is the requirement for the “seven third‑order multiplications” limitation in the ’775 patent, and how did the court determine the evidence was insufficient?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes the patent requires seven specific multiplications of three signals, but the Nokia document only shows three distinct multiplications (and ten total). How must a party prove that the accused device performs the seven multiplications, and why did the court find the expert’s mapping inadequate?

questions.title: How does the Federal Circuit treat expert testimony that is internally contradictory when assessing infringement?
questions.question_body: The court cites Johns Hopkins v. Datascope for rejecting contradictory expert testimony. In this case, Dr. Wells gave conflicting explanations about which signals correspond to the claim elements. What is the legal precedent for evaluating contradictory expert testimony, and what threshold must be met for a jury’s verdict to be supported by substantial evidence?

questions.title: What is the proper procedural basis for granting a new trial on damages after a JMOL of noninfringement is entered?
questions.question_body: The district court denied a new trial on damages, but the appellate court vacated the damages award after reversing the JMOL. If a claim is ultimately found non‑infringing, does a new trial on damages become moot, or are there separate standards for vacating a damages award?

questions.title: Why did the Federal Circuit reverse the district court’s JMOL denial for both the ’134 and ’775 patents, and what does ‘substantial evidence’ mean in this context?
questions.question_body: The opinion repeatedly states the jury’s verdict was not supported by substantial evidence for both patents. I’m trying to understand what level of evidence is required to survive a JMOV (judgment as a matter of view) challenge and how the court applied that standard to the expert’s testimony for each patent.
